research_questions.treatment_description: Alternate-day fasting for 12 months: during weight loss, 25% of energy needs on fast days alternating with 125% on feast days; during maintenance, 50% on fast days alternating with 150% on feast days.
research_questions.control_description: Daily calorie restriction for 12 months: 75% of energy needs each day during the weight-loss phase, followed by 100% of energy needs each day during maintenance.
research_questions.result_section_hint: Results, subsection “Weight Loss and Weight Maintenance,” Table 2, 12-month ADF − DCR comparison
research_questions.evidence_quote: At the end of the study, total weight loss was −6.0% (95% CI, −8.5% to −3.6%) for the alternate-day fasting group and −5.3% (95% CI, −7.6% to −3.0%) for the daily calorie restriction group, relative to controls, with no significant difference between the intervention groups.
research_questions.effect_direction: ADF − DCR = −0.7 percentage points (95% CI, −3.1 to 1.6); no significant difference, numerically favoring alternate-day fasting

content_sections.key_content_summary: Summarizes the 1-year three-arm randomized trial. The primary outcome was change in body weight; alternate-day fasting and daily calorie restriction produced similar weight loss at 6 and 12 months, with no superiority of fasting for adherence, weight maintenance, or cardiovascular risk indicators.

Motivates alternate-day fasting as a potentially easier alternative to daily calorie restriction and reviews short-term weight-loss findings. States hypotheses that alternate-day fasting would improve adherence, weight loss, weight maintenance, and cardiovascular risk indicators more than daily calorie restriction.

Describes recruitment, stratified randomization of 100 adults to alternate-day fasting, daily calorie restriction, or no intervention, the 6-month weight-loss and 6-month maintenance phases, outcome measurement, and intention-to-treat linear mixed-model analysis. Change in body weight was the primary outcome.

Reports attrition, adherence, energy intake, body weight and composition, and cardiovascular risk outcomes. For the eligible comparison, alternate-day fasting versus daily calorie restriction, percentage body-weight change did not differ at 12 months (between-group difference −0.7 percentage points, 95% CI −3.1 to 1.6).

Interprets alternate-day fasting as not superior to daily calorie restriction for adherence, weight loss, maintenance, or cardiovascular risk improvement. Discusses poorer sustainability and higher attrition in the fasting arm, the metabolically healthy sample, and study limitations.
Concludes that alternate-day fasting was not superior to daily calorie restriction for adherence, weight loss, weight maintenance, or cardiovascular risk indicators.
Points to supplementary materials, including the full protocol and supplementary figures and tables cited in the main text.
Provides a structured summary of the main question and finding: 12-month weight loss was 6.0% with alternate-day fasting and 5.3% with daily calorie restriction, with no significant difference.

research_questions.target_construct: percentage change in body weight from baseline
research_questions.primary_outcome: loge relative change in weight between baseline and week 50
research_questions.treatment_description: Intermittent calorie restriction (5:2 diet): two nonconsecutive days per week at 25% of individual energy requirement and five eucaloric days, targeting an approximately 20% weekly energy deficit
research_questions.control_description: Continuous calorie restriction: daily intake at approximately 80% of individual energy requirement, targeting an approximately 20% daily energy deficit
research_questions.result_section_hint: Results, “Sustainability of intervention effects across the maintenance and follow-up phases,” Figure 3 and Supplemental Table 7 (week 50)
research_questions.evidence_quote: Overall, mean loge relative changes in weight between baseline and week 50 were highest for the ICR group (−5.2% ± 1.2%), followed by the CCR (−4.9% ± 1.1%) and control groups (−1.7% ± 0.8%).
research_questions.effect_direction: no significant difference; ICR minus CCR approximately −0.3 percentage points (slightly favors ICR), P = 0.89

content_sections.key_content_summary: Summarizes the 150-participant randomized HELENA trial comparing 5:2 intermittent calorie restriction, continuous calorie restriction, and control. At week 50, percentage weight loss was similar with ICR and CCR (−5.2% versus −4.9%; pairwise P=0.89), with neither regimen superior on metabolic outcomes.

Reviews evidence on intermittent versus continuous calorie restriction and motivates a well-powered long-term comparison. States the hypothesis that ICR may provide greater metabolic benefits than CCR and describes evaluation of sustained changes in weight, body composition, and biomarkers.

Describes an individually randomized, three-arm trial of 150 adults with overweight or obesity, the 5:2 ICR and daily CCR regimens, follow-up through week 50, and intention-to-treat linear mixed models. Adipose-tissue gene expression was primary; percentage body-weight change was a secondary outcome assessed at weeks 12, 24, and 50.

Reports participant flow, adherence, weight, gene expression, biomarkers, body composition, quality of life, and safety. For the synthesis-relevant longest follow-up, week-50 log-relative weight change was −5.2% with ICR and −4.9% with CCR, with no significant ICR–CCR difference.

Interprets ICR and CCR as similarly effective and practicable approaches for weight loss and metabolic improvement over 50 weeks. Notes declining adherence and some weight regain with ICR, but no significant regimen differences in weight or adipose-tissue volumes.
Points to supplemental tables, figures, and methods; the supplied markdown does not reproduce their full contents.

research_questions.primary_outcome: percentage change in body weight by month 6
research_questions.treatment_description: 8-hour time-restricted eating: eating ad libitum from 12:00 pm to 8:00 pm daily without calorie counting for 6 months
research_questions.control_description: Continuous daily calorie restriction: 25% reduction from baseline energy needs with individualized weight-loss meal plans and daily food logging for 6 months
research_questions.result_section_hint: Results, “Weight Loss and Body Composition” and table “Body Weight, Glycemic Control, and Cardiometabolic Risk Factors” (month 6); Discussion opening paragraph
research_questions.evidence_quote: Findings of this randomized clinical trial show that 8-hour TRE produced greater weight loss when compared with CR and a control condition.
research_questions.effect_direction: TRE < CR for percentage weight change (greater weight loss with TRE; favors intermittent fasting)

content_sections.section_title: Abstract (structured: Importance; Objective; Design, Setting, and Participants; Interventions; Main Outcomes and Measures; Results; Conclusions and Relevance)
content_sections.key_content_summary: Reports a 6-month, three-arm randomized clinical trial (N=75) comparing 8-hour time-restricted eating, 25% daily calorie restriction, and control in adults with obesity and type 2 diabetes. The primary outcome was percentage body-weight change at month 6; TRE produced a larger reduction than control, while CR did not significantly differ from control, and HbA1c improved similarly with TRE and CR.

Frames the central question as whether TRE without calorie counting is more effective than daily CR for weight loss and HbA1c lowering. Summarizes weight loss as −3.6% for TRE and −1.8% for CR relative to controls and notes similar HbA1c changes.

Reviews calorie restriction as standard treatment and TRE as a potentially easier alternative for adults with type 2 diabetes. States the hypothesis that TRE would yield greater weight loss and larger HbA1c reductions than CR and control.

content_sections.section_title: Methods (Trial Participants; Randomization and Blinding; Intervention Groups; Medication Management; Blood Glucose Level Monitoring; Outcome Measures; Statistical Analysis)
content_sections.key_content_summary: Describes a 6-month, single-center, 1:1:1 randomized trial of 8-hour TRE, 25% daily CR, and usual-habit control. Percentage body-weight change at month 6 was the primary outcome; intention-to-treat linear mixed models adjusted for baseline medication differences were used, with Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise significance for weight.

content_sections.section_title: Results (Trial Participants; Weight Loss and Body Composition; Glycemic Control and Medication Effect Score; Sensitivity Analysis Using Multiple Imputation; Plasma Lipid Levels and Blood Pressure; Adherence and Energy Intake; Daily Eating Window, Diet Quality, and Physical Activity; Adverse Events)
content_sections.key_content_summary: Among 75 randomized participants, month-6 body weight decreased by −3.56% (95% CI, −5.92% to −1.20%) for TRE and −1.78% (95% CI, −3.67% to 0.11%) for CR, each reported relative to the no-intervention control; the paper states TRE produced greater weight loss than CR. Other reported outcomes include body composition, glycemic measures, cardiometabolic factors, adherence, and adverse events, but these are outside the requested synthesis outcome.

Interprets 8-hour TRE as producing greater weight loss than CR and control, likely aided by better adherence and greater energy restriction. HbA1c reductions were similar with TRE and CR, and the authors discuss applicability and safety in adults with type 2 diabetes.

Notes short duration, lack of participant blinding, baseline imbalances in weight-affecting diabetes medications, and reliance on self-reported dietary intake. Analyses adjusted for baseline medication use.

Concludes that 8-hour TRE without calorie counting may be an effective alternative to daily calorie restriction for weight loss and HbA1c lowering in adults with type 2 diabetes and obesity, while calling for larger and longer trials.

Lists the trial protocol and supplementary files covering medication use, multiple-imputation sensitivity analyses, adverse events, experimental design, intervention adherence, and adherence difficulty. These supplementary analyses are not used as the primary synthesis effect.

research_questions.primary_outcome: weight loss as a percentage of baseline body weight
research_questions.treatment_description: Time-restricted eating without calorie counting: ad libitum intake from noon to 8:00 p.m. during months 0–6, followed by a 10:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. maintenance eating window during months 6–12, with dietary counseling.
research_questions.control_description: Continuous daily calorie restriction: 25% energy restriction during months 0–6 followed by weight-maintenance intake during months 6–12, with dietary counseling.
research_questions.result_section_hint: Results, subsection “Weight Loss and Body Composition”; table titled “Change in Body Weight and Body Composition From Baseline and Between Intervention Groups”
research_questions.evidence_quote: Relative to the control group, weight loss (secondary outcome) as a percentage of baseline body weight was −4.87% (CI, −7.61% to −2.13%) for the TRE group and −5.30% (CI, −9.06% to −1.54%) for the CR group, with no notable difference between the TRE and CR groups (0.43% [CI, −3.48% to 4.34%]) by month 12.
research_questions.effect_direction: TRE − CR = 0.43 percentage points (95% CI, −3.48 to 4.34); no notable difference, point estimate favors calorie restriction

content_sections.section_title: Background: / Objective: / Design: / Setting: / Participants: / Intervention: / Measurements: / Results: / Limitation: / Conclusion:
content_sections.key_content_summary: Structured abstract of a 12-month, three-arm randomized trial in 90 adults with obesity. At month 12, TRE and calorie restriction each reduced weight versus no-intervention control, while TRE did not differ significantly from calorie restriction in absolute or percentage weight change.

content_sections.section_title: Time-restricted eating (TRE) has become a popular weight loss regimen
content_sections.key_content_summary: Reviews the rationale and prior evidence for time-restricted eating, including its potential practicality relative to daily calorie counting. States the hypothesis that TRE would produce greater weight loss and insulin-sensitivity improvements over 12 months than calorie restriction and control.

Describes the 12-month parallel, individually randomized trial of 90 adults with obesity assigned 1:1:1 to TRE, 25% daily calorie restriction, or control. Defines absolute body-weight change as primary and relative body-weight change as a prespecified secondary outcome; analyses used intention-to-treat linear mixed models with robust variance estimates.

Reports participant flow and outcomes. At month 12, percentage weight change relative to control was −4.87 points for TRE and −5.30 points for calorie restriction; the eligible TRE-versus-calorie-restriction contrast was 0.43 percentage points (95% CI, −3.48 to 4.34), indicating no notable difference.

Interprets both TRE without calorie counting and daily calorie restriction as producing greater 12-month weight loss than no-intervention control, with no statistically significant difference between active interventions. Discusses adherence, metabolic findings, applicability to a racially and ethnically diverse population, and study limitations.

content_sections.section_title: In conclusion, TRE is effective for weight loss when compared with controls eating over a period of 10 or more hours but not more effective than daily CR in a racially diverse population.
content_sections.key_content_summary: Concludes that TRE is effective versus no-intervention control but is not more effective than daily calorie restriction; calls for confirmatory studies.

Points to supplementary protocol, CONSORT materials, additional tables and figures, sensitivity analyses, adherence details, and funding/disclosure information; the supplied markdown does not reproduce the supplementary statistical values.

research_questions.target_construct: percentage change in body weight from baseline
research_questions.primary_outcome: percentage body weight loss at six months
research_questions.treatment_description: Intermittent energy-restricted 5:2 diet: 600 calories on two non-consecutive days per week and ad libitum eating on the other five days, for six months.
research_questions.control_description: Standard continuous energy-restricted diet: a 500-calorie daily reduction based on Australian Guide to Healthy Eating principles, for six months.
research_questions.result_section_hint: Results, six-month anthropometric outcomes (also summarized in Abstract)
research_questions.evidence_quote: After six months, mean weight loss for participants on the 5:2 diet was 5.3 ± 3.0 kg (5.5 ± 3.2%) and for participants following the SERD it was 5.5 ± 4.3 kg (5.4 ± 4.2%).
research_questions.effect_direction: no significant between-group difference; 5:2 minus SERD was approximately -0.1 percentage points when weight loss is coded as negative change

content_sections.key_content_summary: Summarizes the six-month randomized comparison of a 5:2 diet with standard daily energy restriction in 24 older men with obesity. Both groups lost about 5.4% of baseline weight, with no significant between-group difference; waist circumference and systolic blood pressure also decreased.

Reviews obesity, intermittent energy restriction, and prior human evidence. States the study aims of testing whether a 5:2 diet achieves 5% weight loss and improves weight and biochemical markers more than standard energy restriction.

Describes a prospectively registered, single-centre parallel RCT of 24 male war veterans aged 55–75 years with obesity, randomized to a 5:2 diet or a 500-calorie/day continuous energy-restricted diet for six months. Outcomes were measured at baseline, three months, and six months, with Wilcoxon tests and robust linear regression used for analysis.

Reports that 23 of 24 participants completed six months. Mean percentage weight loss was 5.5% in the 5:2 group and 5.4% in the standard energy-restriction group, with no significant between-group difference; additional anthropometric, blood-pressure, quality-of-life, adherence, symptom, and dietary results are also presented.

Interprets the 5:2 diet as feasible and as effective, but not superior, to standard daily energy restriction for clinically significant weight loss. Discusses nutritional adequacy, prior intermittent-restriction trials, limitations including small sample size and short duration, and future research needs; the final paragraph gives the paper's conclusion.
Reports grants from the Dietitians Association of Australia and the Austin Hospital Medical Research Foundation.
States that the authors had no conflicts of interest.
Describes author contributions, manuscript approval, and acknowledgments.
Lists the cited literature and guidance documents.

research_questions.target_construct: percentage change in body weight from baseline
research_questions.primary_outcome: percentage of starting weight lost at 12 months
research_questions.treatment_description: Intermittent energy restriction (IER): 500 kcal/day on 2 nonconsecutive days per week, with habitual eating on the other 5 days
research_questions.control_description: Continuous energy restriction (CER): 1500 kcal/day on all 7 days per week
research_questions.result_section_hint: Weight loss section; Table 2 (12-month primary outcome results)
research_questions.evidence_quote: At 12 mo, participants had lost an average (mean SD) of 4.3 ± 5.5% of their starting weight (IER, 5.0 ± 5.4%; CER, 3.5 ± 5.6%; P = 0.3)
research_questions.effect_direction: IER produced greater mean percentage weight loss than CER, but the between-group difference was not statistically significant (direct coding as percentage weight change: IER −5.0% vs CER −3.5%; MD approximately −1.5 percentage points, favoring IER)

content_sections.key_content_summary: Summarizes the 12-month randomized noninferiority comparison of intermittent energy restriction (IER) versus continuous energy restriction (CER) in 121 women with overweight and prior gestational diabetes. Weight decreased over time, with no significant diet-group difference, and diabetes risk markers also did not differ between groups.

Reviews diabetes risk after gestational diabetes, the role of weight loss, and intermittent versus continuous energy restriction. States the hypothesis that 12-month weight loss with IER would not be inferior to CER.
Umbrella heading for the trial methods.
Describes recruitment, eligibility, exclusions, 1:1 randomization, stratification by years since gestational diabetes and BMI, and participant compensation.

Defines IER as 500 kcal/day on two nonconsecutive days weekly and CER as 1500 kcal/day every day, with both designed to provide about 25% weekly energy restriction. Describes dietitian support, records, physical-activity advice, and breastfeeding modifications.

Identifies weight loss as the primary outcome and details body-weight measurement at baseline and follow-ups through 12 months. Also describes secondary glycemic, physical-activity, and sleep measurements.

Describes the noninferiority design, 3.3-kg margin, planned sample size, repeated-measures and nonparametric analyses, and completer plus intention-to-treat analyses. The noninferiority hypothesis applies to the primary weight outcome.
Reports ethics approval, trial registration, and written informed consent.
Reports recruitment, randomization of 121 women, 49% attrition, similar withdrawal by group, and baseline characteristics.

Reports the primary weight outcomes through 12 months. Mean percentage weight loss was 5.0% with IER and 3.5% with CER (P=0.3), while the kilogram-based between-group difference was not significant and fell within the prespecified noninferiority margin.
Reports food-record completion and dietary intake analyses, with no significant between-group changes in energy or macronutrient intake from 3 to 12 months.
Reports HbA1c, glucose, insulin, HOMA-IR, and oral-glucose-tolerance outcomes. Several markers changed over time, but there were no significant diet-by-time differences.
Reports no meaningful between-group differences in physical activity or sleep-quality changes.

Interprets IER as producing weight loss comparable to CER over 12 months and similar changes in diabetes risk markers. Emphasizes that high attrition and the underpowered completion sample limit confidence in noninferiority and implementation.
States that deidentified data may be made available upon request and ethics approval.
Lists cited literature.

research_questions.treatment_description: Intermittent fasting: energy intake restricted to 2510 kJ (600 kcal) during two 24-hour periods per week, with eating to appetite on the other five days, for a 12-week active intervention followed through week 52.
research_questions.control_description: Continuous energy restriction: daily energy intake restricted by 30% relative to estimated weight-maintenance needs, using individualized meal plans, for a 12-week active intervention followed through week 52.
research_questions.evidence_quote: While body weight remained stable within 1 kg during the week 13 to week 52 follow up in both the intermittent fasting group [week 13: 78.8 (65.3–97.6) kg; week 52: 79.6 (66.3–97.6) kg] and the continuous energy restriction group [week 13: 82.6 (73.0–94.6) kg; week 52: 82.3 (67.0–97.8) kg], maintenance of clinically and statistically significant weight loss was only seen in the intermittent fasting group (Table 2).
research_questions.effect_direction: Descriptively favors intermittent fasting at 52 weeks (median change −6.5% vs −2.5%); the paper states there were no between-group differences in outcomes.
research_questions.exclusion_note: Relevant effect identified at the longest eligible follow-up, but Table 2 reports medians and ranges rather than arm-level means with SD/SE/CI, and no between-group estimate with uncertainty is provided; therefore the requested inverse-variance MD cannot be derived from the reported data alone.

content_sections.section_title: ## A B S T R A C T
content_sections.key_content_summary: Summarizes a randomized pilot comparison of intermittent fasting versus continuous energy restriction in 10 adults with type 1 diabetes and overweight/obesity. Both groups lost weight at 12 weeks, with no between-group differences reported; participants were followed to 12 months.

Describes obesity-related risks in type 1 diabetes, limitations of conventional continuous restriction, and the rationale for evaluating intermittent fasting as a potentially safe and effective weight-loss strategy.

Describes a 52-week stratified randomized parallel-group pilot trial with a 12-week active weight-loss phase and follow-up through week 52. Five participants per arm received either two 600-kcal fasting days weekly or continuous 30% energy restriction.
Details protocolized basal and bolus insulin reductions and weekly dose adjustment during the active weight-loss phase.
Describes blood-glucose, continuous-glucose, and ketone monitoring procedures and thresholds for contacting study staff.
Defines outcome collection through week 52, including body weight, DEXA body composition, energy expenditure, blood pressure, HbA1c, and lipids.
States that change from baseline was analyzed by ANOVA with treatment and baseline measurement as covariates; results were expressed as means with SDs or medians with ranges.
Reports recruitment of 10 participants, five per arm, baseline characteristics, and absence of baseline group differences.

Reports unchanged hypoglycaemia frequency and Low Blood Glucose Index, two transient ketone elevations in one intermittent-fasting participant, and one liver-function abnormality judged unrelated to treatment.

Reports significant within-group weight loss at 12 weeks and week-52 percentage weight changes. At week 52, median weight change was −6.5% with intermittent fasting and −2.5% with continuous restriction; only intermittent fasting retained statistically significant within-group loss.

Interprets intermittent fasting as a potentially safe, effective, and tolerable alternative to continuous restriction for adults with type 1 diabetes and overweight/obesity, while emphasizing glucose monitoring and treatment adjustment.
States that no relevant potential conflicts of interest were reported.
Lists author roles in data collection, analysis, writing, discussion, and manuscript review.
Reports support from a Novo Nordisk Regional Diabetes Support Scheme Grant.
Provides a link to online supplementary data.
Lists cited literature on intermittent fasting, energy restriction, diabetes, obesity, and related methods.

research_questions.target_construct: percentage change in body weight from baseline
research_questions.primary_outcome: Weight, kg (change from baseline at month 12; convertible to percentage change using baseline weight)
research_questions.treatment_description: Time-restricted eating: prescribed calorie intake consumed only from 8:00 AM to 4:00 PM daily for 12 months (1500–1800 kcal/day for men and 1200–1500 kcal/day for women).
research_questions.control_description: Daily calorie restriction with the same prescribed calorie targets for 12 months but habitual meal timing and no eating-time restriction.
research_questions.result_section_hint: Results, subsection “Weight Loss and Body Fat,” Table 2, Month 12 weight row
research_questions.evidence_quote: During the 12-month intervention, body weight was significantly reduced by 8.4 kg (95% CI, −10.3 to −6.4 kg) in the TRE group and 7.8 kg (95% CI, −9.7 to −5.9 kg) in the DCR group, with no significant between-group differences (−0.6 kg; 95% CI, −3.3 to 2.2 kg; P = .69) (Table 2; eFigure 2 in Supplement 2).
research_questions.effect_direction: no significant difference; point estimate favors TRE (greater weight loss)

content_sections.key_content_summary: Summarizes the 12-month randomized comparison of time-restricted eating (TRE) versus daily calorie restriction (DCR) in 88 adults with obesity and NAFLD. TRE did not provide additional benefit for intrahepatic triglycerides, body weight, body fat, or metabolic risk factors.

States the clinical question and central finding: 12-month reductions in liver fat occurred in both groups, without significant between-group differences; TRE also did not add benefit for body fat or major metabolic risk factors.

Reviews NAFLD, caloric restriction, and prior evidence on TRE, then identifies uncertainty about whether food timing adds benefit beyond calorie restriction. The authors hypothesized that 8-hour TRE would outperform DCR for NAFLD and metabolic risk factors.

Describes the observer-blinded, parallel-group RCT; eligibility and randomization; TRE and DCR interventions; adherence; MRI liver-fat and secondary anthropometric/metabolic outcomes; and intention-to-treat linear mixed-model analyses. Both arms received the same calorie targets, while only TRE restricted eating to 8 AM–4 PM.

Reports enrollment, retention, adherence, and all efficacy and safety findings. At 12 months, weight decreased by 8.4 kg with TRE and 7.8 kg with DCR, with no significant between-group difference (−0.6 kg, 95% CI −3.3 to 2.2; P=.69).

Interprets TRE as no more effective than isoenergetic DCR for liver fat, weight, body composition, or most metabolic outcomes. The authors argue that calorie restriction likely explains most benefits of TRE and compare the findings with prior trials.
Notes that liver fat rather than biopsy-confirmed steatosis or fibrosis was the primary endpoint and that physical activity was assessed but not controlled.
Concludes that TRE added no benefit over DCR for liver fat, weight, body fat, or most metabolic risk factors, emphasizing calorie restriction in NAFLD management.
Provides publication details, author affiliations and contributions, conflicts, funding, funder role, data sharing, and acknowledgments.
Lists cited literature on NAFLD, calorie restriction, intermittent fasting, TRE, obesity, metabolic risk, and outcome measurement.

Identifies the trial protocol and statistical analysis plan, supplementary adherence and sensitivity tables, adverse events, subgroup and weight figures, and the data-sharing statement; their full contents are not reproduced in the supplied markdown.

research_questions.primary_outcome: Weight (%) change from baseline to 6 months
research_questions.treatment_description: Six-month, 16-session faith-based 5:2 intermittent-fasting intervention: two fasting days per week with one 500-kcal meal on each fasting day and healthy eating on the other five days, delivered by community health workers in Black churches.
research_questions.control_description: Six-month, 16-session faith-based continuous energy restriction intervention (The WORD), providing standard behavioral weight-loss education and daily calorie-restriction guidance, delivered by community health workers in Black churches.
research_questions.result_section_hint: Table 2; RESULTS subsection “Changes in body weight and other anthropometric measures (Table 2)”
research_questions.evidence_quote: Participants in the IF arm lost −3.5 (95% CI: −6, −0.9)% of their baseline body weight from baseline to 6 months.
research_questions.effect_direction: No significant between-group difference; adjusted IF minus CER estimate −0.5 percentage points (95% CI −3.8 to 2.8), numerically favoring IF.

content_sections.key_content_summary: Summarizes a cluster-randomized pilot comparing a 6-month 5:2 intermittent-fasting intervention with continuous energy restriction in 42 Black adults. Feasibility was the primary outcome; both arms lost weight, with no claim of superior percentage weight loss for intermittent fasting.

Motivates intermittent fasting as a potentially scalable alternative to continuous calorie restriction for Black adults and states the hypotheses that both interventions would produce significant weight loss and that IF would produce comparable weight loss to CER.

Describes the community partnership, intervention development, cluster-randomized design, recruitment, measures, sample-size calculation, and analysis. Five churches and 42 adults were randomized to 6 months of 5:2 IF or CER; linear mixed models adjusted for baseline outcome and within-church clustering, with intent-to-treat multiple imputation.

Reports recruitment and retention, participant characteristics, changes in anthropometric and behavioral outcomes, biomarkers, adherence, and acceptance. At 6 months, percentage body-weight change was −3.5% with IF and −2.9% with CER; the clustering-adjusted between-group estimate was −0.5 percentage points (95% CI −3.8 to 2.8), indicating no significant difference.

Interprets the significant and comparable within-arm weight losses, dietary findings, adherence, biomarker patterns, limitations, and implications. The authors emphasize the pilot's small sample and the need for larger studies.
Concludes that the 5:2 IF intervention was feasible in Black churches and yielded preliminary weight loss comparable to CER, while calling for larger scalable trials.
Directs readers to supplementary material on PubMed Central; the supplied markdown does not include the supplementary analyses themselves.
Restates the feasibility research question and key findings, including no observed IF–CER difference in weight loss and differences in dietary intake and self-monitoring adherence.

research_questions.target_construct: percentage change in body weight from baseline
research_questions.treatment_description: Time-restricted eating restricted intake to 1000–1900 h for six months, with four timing-focused consultations and no dietary-content advice.
research_questions.control_description: Individualized standard dietetic guidance for type 2 diabetes for six months, delivered in four time-matched consultations covering diet quality and quantity, carbohydrate, label reading, and alcohol.
research_questions.result_section_hint: Section 3. Results, body-composition paragraph and Fig. 3A
research_questions.evidence_quote: A main effect of time was measured for BM (Fig. 3A), where the TRE group had a reduced BM after the intervention (−1.7 kg, P=0.01) with a smaller reduction in DIET (−1.2 kg, P=0.14).
research_questions.effect_direction: TRE showed greater mean weight loss than DIET at 6 months; no group-by-time effect was reported. Using reported completer baseline body mass, approximate percentage changes are −1.93% for TRE (−1.7/87.9×100) and −1.20% for DIET (−1.2/100.2×100), giving an unadjusted MD of approximately −0.74 percentage points.
research_questions.exclusion_note: The six-month contrast is eligible, but the main text provides no SD/SE/CI for arm-level weight change and no between-group change estimate with uncertainty; therefore it cannot contribute to the planned inverse-variance meta-analysis from the reported text alone.

content_sections.section_title: ## A B S T R A C T
content_sections.key_content_summary: Reports a six-month parallel-group RCT comparing 9-hour time-restricted eating (TRE) with individualized dietetic guidance in adults with type 2 diabetes and overweight/obesity. HbA1c was the primary outcome; both groups lost modest body mass (TRE −1.7 kg; DIET −1.2 kg), while TRE was non-inferior for HbA1c and had higher self-reported adherence.

Reviews dietetic care and time-restricted eating for type 2 diabetes, including evidence on glycaemia and weight. States the aim of comparing TRE with standard individualized dietetic guidance and hypothesizes comparable efficacy for glycaemic management.

Describes the registered, randomized parallel-group trial, eligibility, monitoring, interventions, dietary and biochemical measurements, and statistical analysis. Participants were randomized to TRE (eating 1000–1900 h) or time-matched individualized dietary counseling for six months; body composition was measured at baseline, two months, and six months, with HbA1c prespecified as primary.

Reports outcomes for 51 randomized and 43 completing participants. For the synthesis-relevant weight outcome, body mass declined by 1.7 kg in TRE and 1.2 kg in DIET at six months; the paper reports a time effect but does not provide an SD/SE/CI for arm-level weight change or a between-group weight-change estimate with uncertainty.

Interprets comparable glycaemic improvements under TRE and standard dietetic care. Notes spontaneous energy restriction and clinically insignificant (<5%) and variable weight losses in both groups, with higher adherence to TRE, and discusses implementation and limitations.
Lists author roles in study conception, design, conduct, analysis, interpretation, and manuscript preparation.
States that portions of the work were previously presented at two 2023 diabetes conferences.
Provides detailed contributor-role taxonomy assignments for each author.
Reports support from a Diabetes Australia Research Program grant and Australian Catholic University return-to-work grants.
Discloses financial support to the lead author and states that the remaining authors report no relevant competing interests.
Thanks research staff for assistance with dietary analyses and laboratory measurements.
Provides the DOI link to supplementary material containing additional figures and tables.

research_questions.target_construct: percentage change in body weight from baseline
research_questions.primary_outcome: change in bodyweight after the subsequent 3-month follow-up
research_questions.treatment_description: Three months of self-selected 10-h per-day time-restricted eating, followed by three months without active intervention; participants were also advised to follow the Danish Official Dietary Guidelines.
research_questions.control_description: Habitual living during the three-month intervention, followed by three months without active intervention; participants were advised to follow the Danish Official Dietary Guidelines.
research_questions.evidence_quote: Being in the TRE group was not associated with a lower bodyweight compared with the control group after the subsequent 3-month follow-up period (–0·2 kg, 95% CI –1·6 to 1·2).
research_questions.effect_direction: no significant difference; TRE minus control = −0.2 kg (95% CI −1.6 to 1.2) at approximately 6 months, corresponding to about −0.20 percentage points (95% CI −1.57 to 1.18) when converted using the model baseline weight of 101.8 kg

content_sections.key_content_summary: Summarises the RESET randomised trial of 10-h/day time-restricted eating versus habitual living in 100 adults at high risk of type 2 diabetes. The primary bodyweight contrast was not significant at 3 months, and the difference remained small at the 3-month post-intervention follow-up.

Introduces time-restricted eating as a potentially feasible weight-management strategy and reviews proposed mechanisms. States the hypothesis that 3 months of TRE would induce clinically relevant weight loss and that this loss would be maintained during follow-up.

Places the study in the prior TRE literature, noting the scarcity of randomised trials without caloric restrictions and of trials with follow-up. Concludes that this trial adds evidence that 10-h TRE did not significantly reduce bodyweight compared with habitual living.
Describes the literature search and identifies six earlier relevant clinical trials, most of which were small pilot studies or combined TRE with controlled diets.

Highlights the randomised design, high-risk overweight/obese population, repeated glucose monitoring, and predefined follow-up. States that TRE did not significantly reduce bodyweight despite high adherence.

content_sections.section_title: ## Implications of all the available evidence
content_sections.key_content_summary: States that 10-h TRE cannot be recommended as a short-term clinically relevant weight-loss strategy for this population and calls for longer-term studies in more metabolically impaired populations.
Umbrella methods section for study design, eligibility, randomisation, intervention procedures, outcomes, and statistical analysis.
Describes a single-centre, parallel, superiority, open-label randomised controlled trial conducted at Steno Diabetes Center Copenhagen with ethics and data-protection approval.
Defines recruitment, consent, and eligibility criteria for adults aged 30–70 years with overweight plus prediabetes or obesity, and a habitual eating window sufficiently long for TRE restriction.
Describes 1:1 block randomisation to 10-h TRE or habitual living, concealment during baseline assessment, open treatment allocation, and masking of outcome assessors during analysis.

Details the self-selected 10-h eating window, habitual-living control, Danish dietary-guideline advice, intervention and follow-up visits, anthropometry, metabolic assessments, and adherence monitoring.

Defines change in bodyweight at the end of the 3-month intervention and after the subsequent 3-month follow-up as the primary outcome; identifies body composition, energy intake, glycaemic measures, and LDL cholesterol as secondary outcomes.

Reports the power calculation and specifies baseline-adjusted linear mixed models for intention-to-treat analysis, a per-protocol analysis for bodyweight, hierarchical testing for the primary outcome, and FDR correction for secondary outcomes.
States that the funder had no role in study design, conduct, analysis, interpretation, or manuscript preparation.

Reports enrolment, retention, adherence, and primary and secondary outcomes. At the longest eligible follow-up (about 6 months after randomisation), the adjusted bodyweight difference for TRE versus control was −0.2 kg (95% CI −1.6 to 1.2), with no evidence of maintained benefit.

Interprets the trial as showing no clinically relevant weight loss or cardiometabolic improvement from 3 months of 10-h TRE, despite high retention and intervention adherence. Discusses prior TRE trials, possible compensation in energy intake, reduced adherence during follow-up, strengths, limitations, and generalisability.
Lists author contributions to study conception, design, data collection, analysis, interpretation, funding, and manuscript preparation.
Discloses funding, employment, equity, consulting, speaking, and other potential competing interests of the authors.
States that anonymised aggregate data are available on reasonable request but individual participant data cannot be shared under the consent terms.
Acknowledges funding sources, study participants, and personnel who assisted with trial conduct and data analysis.
Provides the cited literature on TRE, obesity, metabolic health, trial methods, and qualitative companion studies.

research_questions.treatment_description: Intermittent fasting (IMF): approximately 20% of estimated weight-maintenance caloric needs on three non-consecutive fasting days per week, delivered as a behavioral weight-loss intervention for 12 months
research_questions.control_description: Daily caloric restriction (DCR): continuous daily caloric restriction delivered as a behavioral weight-loss intervention for 12 months
research_questions.result_section_hint: Results, Human study, “Feasibility, safety, acceptability, and tolerability,” p. 2; Figure 1A, p. 4
research_questions.evidence_quote: At 12 months, participants in the DCR group had lost additional weight (−9.1 ± 6.0%) while weight loss in the IMF group plateaued (−4.9 ± 5.6%; p < 0.05 versus DCR at 12 months).
research_questions.effect_direction: IMF > DCR for percentage weight change (less weight loss with IMF); favors DCR

content_sections.key_content_summary: Summarizes parallel human and mouse studies of caloric restriction and fasting in ADPKD. In humans, both daily caloric restriction (DCR) and intermittent fasting (IMF) produced clinically significant weight loss, but DCR produced greater weight loss and better adherence/tolerability.

Reviews ADPKD progression, obesity and metabolic dysregulation, and dietary approaches including DCR, time-restricted feeding, and IMF. Introduces a one-year randomized human feasibility trial comparing DCR with IMF and a parallel mouse experiment.

Reports the human and animal trial findings. For the synthesis-relevant human outcome, percent weight change was −7.1% with DCR and −5.5% with IMF at 3 months, and −9.1% with DCR versus −4.9% with IMF at 12 months, with a significant group-by-time difference at 12 months; the remaining results concern adherence, safety, imaging, biomarkers, and mouse PKD outcomes.

Interprets DCR as more feasible and effective for sustained weight loss than IMF in adults with overweight/obesity and ADPKD. Discusses exploratory kidney-growth findings, complementary mouse evidence, potential mechanisms, and the possible importance of weight loss rather than fasting alone.

Notes that the human trial was a small pilot feasibility study with no untreated control, exploratory htTKV analyses, no human TRF arm, and no multiple-comparison adjustment for exploratory outcomes; the mouse model was not obese.

Lists the methods components and provides the key resources table for human samples, mouse models, assays, software, and other materials. The supplied markdown references detailed human/animal methods and statistical analysis but does not reproduce those detailed subsections.
Points readers to the online supplemental information associated with the article DOI.

research_questions.treatment_description: Intermittent fasting plus early time-restricted eating (iTRE): 30% of baseline energy requirements consumed between approximately 0800 and 1200 hours, followed by a 20-hour fast, on three nonconsecutive days per week; usual ad libitum diet on nonfasting days.
research_questions.control_description: Continuous daily calorie restriction (CR): 30% restriction of calculated baseline energy requirements each day, with no prescribed meal timing.
research_questions.result_section_hint: Results—Body weight and composition; Table 3, month 6 (p. 969)
research_questions.evidence_quote: Body weight and fat mass loss were greater in both iTRE and CR versus standard care over the first 6 months (Table 3). There were no detectable differences in weight trajectories between the iTRE and CR groups (Supplementary Table 2 and Extended Data Figs. 2 and 3).
research_questions.effect_direction: No statistically significant difference; point estimates favored iTRE (month-6 change: −7.59% versus −6.99% with CR; iTRE minus CR approximately −0.60 percentage points; P = 0.28).

content_sections.key_content_summary: Summarizes the three-arm randomized trial and identifies change in mixed-meal glucose AUC at month 6 as the primary outcome. It reports greater glycemic improvement with iTRE than calorie restriction at 6 months, with differences absent by month 18.

Reviews intermittent fasting, calorie restriction, and meal-timing evidence, then motivates testing intermittent fasting plus early time-restricted eating against daily calorie restriction and standard care in adults at elevated type 2 diabetes risk.

Reports participant flow and outcomes for glycemic control, cardiovascular and liver markers, body weight and composition, diet and activity, 18-month follow-up, exploratory analyses, and safety. For the synthesis outcome, month-6 percentage body-weight change was −7.59% with iTRE and −6.99% with daily calorie restriction, with no detectable iTRE–CR difference (P=0.28).

Interprets iTRE as superior to calorie restriction for the primary postprandial glycemia outcome but similar for weight and body composition. Discusses adherence, safety, possible mechanisms, limitations, and the loss of intervention benefits by month 18.
Concludes that iTRE provided a modest 6-month postprandial glycemia benefit over daily calorie restriction and suggests meal timing and fasting advice may matter clinically.

Describes the open-label three-arm parallel randomized trial, eligibility and randomization, iTRE/CR/standard-care interventions, body-weight and metabolic outcome measurement, sample-size considerations, and adjusted regression methods. The intervention phase lasted 6 months, followed by a 12-month follow-up.
Directs readers to the online methods, supplementary information, reporting summaries, source data, acknowledgements, peer review, and data/code availability materials.

research_questions.treatment_description: Time-restricted eating (TRE): eating within an 8-hour window beginning within 3 hours of waking, alongside healthy-eating guidance, for 12 months
research_questions.control_description: Healthy-eating advice without any time restriction (HE) for 12 months
research_questions.result_section_hint: RESULTS — Clinical measurements and self-reported questionnaires; Figure 1A
research_questions.evidence_quote: At month 12, the TRE group lost 2.4 ± 6.4% body weight and the HE group lost 3.6 ± 5.4% body weight (P = .66) (Fig. 1).
research_questions.effect_direction: TRE lost less weight than HE; no significant difference (intermittent fasting minus regular dietary advice MD = +1.2 percentage points)

content_sections.key_content_summary: Summarizes the 12-month randomized comparison of time-restricted eating (TRE) versus healthy-eating advice (HE) in 29 adults with ADPKD. Reports adherence, eating-window duration, percentage weight change, annual htTKV change, and correlations of weight/adiposity change with htTKV.
Graphically summarizes completion, eating-window duration, modest weight loss, and the conclusion that weight/adiposity loss may matter more for kidney growth than eating timing.
States prior evidence, the study's contribution, and implications. Highlights similar modest weight loss in TRE and HE and no randomized-group differences in anthropometric or metabolic changes.

Reviews metabolic mechanisms in ADPKD and rationale for fasting/TRE. States the hypothesis that TRE would be acceptable and produce greater weight loss, more favorable body composition, and improved metabolic outcomes than HE after one year.

Describes the one-year randomized, two-arm pilot trial, participants, TRE and HE interventions, adherence primary endpoint, clinical and exploratory measurements, MRI, and statistical analysis. The prespecified feasibility hypothesis was that 75% of TRE participants would adhere to the 8-hour window.

Reports participant flow, adherence and safety, anthropometric and clinical outcomes, and dietary intake. At 12 months, percentage weight loss was 2.4% in TRE and 3.6% in HE, with no significant between-group difference (P=.66).

Interprets the feasibility and efficacy findings, including similar modest 12-month weight loss in TRE and HE, limited adherence and separation in eating windows, and no difference in annual htTKV change. Discusses limitations and concludes that larger efficacy trials are needed.
Directs readers to supplementary data available online.
Lists study funding sources and investigator support.
States that underlying data will be shared on reasonable request to the corresponding author.
Discloses that K.L. Nowak has consulted for Otsuka.
Provides the ClinicalTrials.gov registration number NCT04534985.

research_questions.target_construct: percentage change in body weight from baseline
research_questions.treatment_description: Hypoenergetic diet plus daily 12-hour time-restricted feeding (HD+TRF) for 12 months
research_questions.control_description: The same hypoenergetic diet without time restriction (HD) for 12 months
research_questions.result_section_hint: Section 3. Results, Table 2 (intention-to-treat analysis), Weight loss (%) row
research_questions.evidence_quote: In the intention-to-treat analysis comparing final means, after 12 months of intervention, there were no significant differences in body weight, body composition, and vital signs between groups (Table 2).
research_questions.effect_direction: HD+TRF − HD = -0.08 percentage points (95% CI -2.86 to 2.69; p=0.95), no significant difference; point estimate favors time-restricted feeding

content_sections.section_title: ## s u m m a r y
content_sections.key_content_summary: Summarizes the 12-month randomized trial of a hypoenergetic diet plus 12-hour time-restricted feeding versus the same diet without time restriction. The primary body-weight outcome showed no between-group effect; secondary body-fat, waist-circumference, and axillary-temperature findings were also summarized.

Reviews obesity prevalence, dietary adherence, intermittent fasting and time-restricted feeding evidence, and gaps in long-term controlled research. States that the primary objective was to assess long-term TRF effects on body weight, with body composition and vital signs as secondary outcomes.

Describes a 12-month parallel randomized controlled trial in 58 low-income adult women with obesity. Participants received either an energy-restricted diet plus a self-selected 12-hour feeding window or the same energy-restricted diet without time restriction; outcomes and intention-to-treat and per-protocol analyses are specified.

Reports participant flow, baseline characteristics, attrition, and outcome comparisons. At 12 months, intention-to-treat percentage weight change was -0.77% for HD+TRF and -0.69% for HD, with a between-group difference of -0.08 percentage points (95% CI -2.86 to 2.69; p=0.95), indicating no effect on weight loss.

Interprets the absence of a significant body-weight effect and discusses secondary body-fat, waist-circumference, and temperature findings. Notes substantial attrition, the intention-to-treat imputation approach, limited clinical importance of secondary findings, and strengths and limitations.
Concludes that TRF did not significantly affect weight loss in low-income women with obesity, while decreases in waist circumference and body-fat percentage were not clinically meaningful.
Identifies partial support from FAPEAL and a CAPES research grant.
States that the authors declare no conflict of interest.
Thanks collaborators for access to indirect-calorimetry and bioimpedance equipment.
Points readers to supplementary data hosted online with the article.

research_questions.target_construct: percentage change in body weight from baseline
research_questions.treatment_description: Zero-calorie alternate-day fasting (ADF) for 8 weeks, followed by 24 weeks of unsupervised follow-up
research_questions.control_description: Moderate daily caloric restriction (CR; prescribed 400 kcal/day deficit) for 8 weeks, followed by 24 weeks of unsupervised follow-up
research_questions.result_section_hint: Body Weight and Body Composition (Table 4), baseline to week 32
research_questions.evidence_quote: Between baseline and the end of the 24-week follow-up (baseline to week 32) there were no differences in absolute or relative weight change (Table 4) and differences in change in absolute FM (CR -2.5±1.1 kg, ADF -4.2±1.0 kg), trunk FM (CR -1.3±0.7 kg, ADF -2.7±0.6 kg), or LM (CR -1.6±0.6 kg, ADF -1.2±0.6 kg) did not reach statistical significance.
research_questions.effect_direction: ADF produced 1.5 percentage points greater weight loss than CR at week 32 (ADF -5.9% vs CR -4.4%; intermittent fasting minus regular dietary advice MD = -1.5 percentage points), but the difference was not significant (p=0.496).

content_sections.key_content_summary: Randomized pilot trial comparing 8 weeks of zero-calorie alternate-day fasting (ADF) with moderate daily caloric restriction (CR) in adults with obesity. It reports similar weight, body-composition, lipid, and insulin-sensitivity changes at 8 weeks and no significant difference in weight regain after 24 weeks of unsupervised follow-up.

Reviews intermittent fasting and the lack of randomized comparisons against standard daily calorie restriction. States that safety/tolerability was the primary aim and that efficacy for weight, body composition, lipids, insulin sensitivity, and later weight regain was secondary; hypothesizes greater weight loss with ADF and no increased regain.

content_sections.section_title: ## Methods (including Participants, Experimental Design, Outcome Measures, Safety Assessments, and Statistical Analyses)
content_sections.key_content_summary: Describes adult eligibility, sex-stratified randomization, the 8-week food-provided ADF versus CR intervention, and 24-week unsupervised follow-up. Body weight was measured at baseline, week 8, and week 32; efficacy was assessed with linear mixed-effects models including time, group, and time-by-group interaction.

content_sections.section_title: ## Results (including Study Enrollment and Attrition; Participant Characteristics; Safety; Energy Intake; Body Weight and Body Composition; RMR; Lipids and Insulin Sensitivity; Leptin, Ghrelin, and BDNF)
content_sections.key_content_summary: Twenty-six participants completed the intervention and 21 completed follow-up. Percentage weight change did not significantly differ between ADF and CR at week 8 or week 32; at week 32, changes were -5.9% for ADF and -4.4% for CR (between-group p=0.496). Other sections report body composition, metabolic, hormonal, and safety findings that are outside the requested synthesis outcome.

Interprets ADF as safe, tolerable, and broadly equivalent to moderate CR for short-term weight loss. Notes that ADF did not increase weight regain during follow-up, while emphasizing the pilot sample, baseline weight imbalance, limited power, and lack of adherence data during unsupervised follow-up.

Concludes that zero-calorie ADF produced weight loss similar to moderate daily CR and was not associated with greater regain after 24 weeks of unsupervised follow-up. Recommends larger and longer efficacy trials.

Summarizes prior knowledge and the study's contribution: ADF and CR yielded similar changes in weight and other measures at 8 weeks, and weight regain after 24 weeks of follow-up did not differ between groups.

research_questions.target_construct: percentage change in body weight from baseline at 12 months
research_questions.primary_outcome: change in body weight after one year
research_questions.treatment_description: Intermittent energy restriction: 400 kcal/day for women or 600 kcal/day for men on two non-consecutive days per week, with usual intake on the other five days
research_questions.control_description: Continuous energy restriction: an equivalent weekly energy reduction distributed evenly across seven days
research_questions.result_section_hint: ## Results — ## Study outcomes; Table 2; one-year values additionally reported in the Abstract
research_questions.evidence_quote: Overall, weight loss was similar among participants in the intermittent versus continuous energy restriction group after one year (8.0 kg [SD 6.5] versus 9.0 kg [SD 7.1]; p Z 0.6) as were changes in waist circumference (8.7 cm [SD 5.9] versus 9.6 cm [SD 6.3]; p Z 1.0).
research_questions.effect_direction: no significant difference; after conversion from kg loss using baseline weights, mean percentage weight change was approximately -7.37% for intermittent restriction and -8.37% for continuous restriction (intermittent minus continuous MD approximately +1.01 percentage points, favoring continuous restriction by coding convention)

content_sections.key_content_summary: Randomized 112 adults with abdominal obesity to intermittent 5:2-style energy restriction or equivalent continuous restriction. At one year, weight loss was similar (8.0 vs 9.0 kg; p=0.6), as were weight maintenance and cardiometabolic improvements, while hunger was higher with intermittent restriction.

Reviews limitations of continuous calorie restriction, intermittent-fasting approaches, prior trials and meta-analyses, and the clinical relevance of metabolic syndrome. States the aim of comparing intermittent versus continuous energy restriction for weight loss, maintenance, and cardiometabolic risk over one year.

Describes eligibility, stratified block randomization, the 6-month weight-loss and 6-month maintenance phases, intermittent restriction (400/600 kcal for women/men on two nonconsecutive days weekly), equivalent continuous daily restriction, measurements, and analysis. The primary endpoint was change in body weight after one year; intent-to-treat repeated-measures mixed ANOVA was the primary between-group approach.

Reports high retention and similar one-year weight loss with intermittent and continuous restriction (8.0 vs 9.0 kg; p=0.6), with no between-group differences in maintenance or cardiometabolic outcomes. Also reports energy intake, activity, adverse events, resting metabolic rate, and greater hunger with intermittent restriction.

Interprets the 5:2 intervention as similarly effective, but not superior, to continuous restriction for clinically significant weight loss, maintenance, and cardiometabolic improvement. Discusses hunger, adherence, generalizability, strengths, and limitations.
Concludes that intermittent and continuous restriction achieved similar weight loss and cardiometabolic improvements and calls for trials lasting at least two years.

content_sections.section_title: ## Statement of author contributions to the manuscript
content_sections.key_content_summary: Lists each author's roles in study design, counselling, supervision, analysis, manuscript preparation, and final-content responsibility.
Reports no conflicts of interest.
Acknowledges staff who assisted with counselling, examinations, metabolic measurements, and study procedures.
Provides the link to supplementary material associated with the article.

research_questions.treatment_description: Alternate-day modified fasting (ADMF): a 600–850 kcal/day very-low-energy diet on 2–3 days per week with healthy-eating guidance on other days, plus remotely delivered exercise and behavioral support, for 24 weeks.
research_questions.control_description: Continuous daily energy restriction with a 1200–1600 kcal/day low-calorie diet (LCD), plus the same remotely delivered exercise and behavioral support, for 24 weeks.
research_questions.result_section_hint: Section 3.3, pp. 5–6; Table 2, p. 8; Figure 3, p. 9
research_questions.evidence_quote: Both LCD (−9.9 ± 6.9 kg; p = 0.03) and ADMF (−13.7 ± 4.8 kg; p = 0.02) produced clinically relevant weight loss (Table 2; Figure 3A,B).
research_questions.effect_direction: ADMF produced greater percentage weight loss than LCD descriptively (−13.9% vs −10.7% at 24 weeks; intermittent fasting minus regular dietary advice ≈ −3.2 percentage points), with no inferential between-group test reported.

content_sections.key_content_summary: Summarizes a 24-week randomized pilot trial of alternate-day modified fasting (ADMF) versus a continuous low-calorie diet (LCD), both with exercise, in adults with obesity and compensated cirrhosis. Reports completion, weight loss, body-composition changes, and functional improvement.

Explains the risks of obesity, sarcopenia, and fat-free-mass loss in cirrhosis and motivates ADMF as a potentially muscle-sparing weight-loss strategy. States that feasibility was the primary aim and body-composition effects were secondary.

Describes the 24-week parallel randomized trial, eligibility criteria, ADMF and continuous LCD interventions, shared exercise and behavioral support, anthropometry/DXA and functional assessments, and analysis using medians, adjusted MADs, and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.

Reports that 13 participants were analyzed at 24 weeks (ADMF n=7; LCD n=6). Median percentage weight change was −13.9% with ADMF and −10.7% with LCD; both groups also showed reductions in weight/BMI and changes in body composition and chair-stand performance.

Interprets both dietary approaches as feasible and capable of clinically meaningful weight loss, while noting larger-than-targeted fat-free-mass losses. Emphasizes pilot-study limitations, especially small sample size and insufficient power for between-group differences, and calls for larger efficacy trials.
Lists author roles in conceptualization, methods, execution, statistical analysis, and manuscript preparation.
Identifies institutional and grant support for the trial.
States that the authors declare no conflicts of interest.
Provides ORCID identifiers for three authors.
Lists cited literature on cirrhosis, sarcopenia, exercise, nutrition, intermittent fasting, and weight management.

research_questions.primary_outcome: % weight change from baseline at week 39 by DXA
research_questions.treatment_description: Early time-restricted eating within a 10-hour window starting within 3 hours of waking, plus approximately 35% daily caloric restriction and behavioral weight-loss support (E-TRE+DCR).
research_questions.control_description: Approximately 35% continuous daily caloric restriction with behavioral weight-loss support and no prescribed eating-time restriction (DCR).
research_questions.result_section_hint: Results, “Body weight and composition by DXA”; Table 3; Figure 3D
research_questions.evidence_quote: At week 39, the DCR group lost −4.3 (5.3) kg (−4.7 [5.7] %), while the E-TRE group lost −4.9 (5.3) kg (−5.2 [5.9] %). There were no between-group differences in weight, FM or FFM at week 39 (p=0.62, p=0.93 and p=0.39, respectively).
research_questions.effect_direction: E-TRE+DCR showed 0.5 percentage points more mean weight loss than DCR, but the between-group difference was not statistically significant (p=0.62).

content_sections.key_content_summary: Randomized trial of E-TRE plus daily caloric restriction versus daily caloric restriction alone in 81 adults with obesity. Weight loss did not differ at weeks 12 or 39, and no between-group differences were found for body composition, energy intake, HbA1c, or lipids.

Reviews evidence on time-restricted eating, meal timing, weight loss, and metabolic outcomes. States the hypothesis that E-TRE+DCR would be acceptable and yield greater weight loss and more favorable body-composition and metabolic changes than DCR.
Introduces the trial methods, with detailed subsections on participants, randomization, interventions, outcomes, power, and statistical analysis.
Defines eligibility as adults aged 18–50 years with BMI 27–45 kg/m², stable weight, and habitual eating duration over 12 hours; reports ethics approval and registration NCT03571048.
Describes 1:1 randomization to E-TRE+DCR or DCR, a 39-week behavioral intervention, calorie goals, a 10-hour early eating window for E-TRE, and COVID-related measurement modifications.
Describes questionnaire-based adherence assessments at baseline and weeks 4, 8, and 12.
Describes assessment of energy-intake timing using photographic food records.
Details digital-scale and DXA measurement of weight and body composition at baseline, week 12, and week 39, including home-scale procedures during COVID-19.

content_sections.section_title: Energy Intake and Healthy Eating Index:
content_sections.key_content_summary: Describes 3-day photographic food records for energy intake and derivation of the Healthy Eating Index.
Describes visual analogue scale appetite measures and Three Factor Eating Inventory outcomes.
Describes fasting indirect-calorimetry assessment of resting energy expenditure at baseline and week 12.
Describes 7-day activPAL accelerometry and derived physical-activity and sedentary-behavior measures.
Describes laboratory measurement of HbA1c and lipid outcomes at baseline and week 12.

content_sections.section_title: Sample Size Determination and Power Analysis:
content_sections.key_content_summary: Identifies 12-week weight change as the prespecified primary outcome and reports power to detect a 2.2-kg between-group difference with a target enrollment of 80.
Specifies intent-to-treat random-intercept mixed models with time, randomized group, and interaction fixed effects, using contrasts for within- and between-group differences.
Introduces the trial results, including participant flow, adherence, meal timing, weight, body composition, diet, activity, energy expenditure, and metabolic outcomes.
Reports enrollment, baseline comparability, and retention: 85 enrolled, with 86% retained at week 12 and 78% at week 39.

Reports no significant between-group differences in calorie-goal adherence, perceived adherence, difficulty, or class attendance; E-TRE participants adhered more successfully to eating windows than calorie goals.
E-TRE+DCR produced a shorter eating duration and earlier last meal than DCR at week 12; both groups shortened eating duration.

content_sections.section_title: ## Body weight by clinic or home scale:
content_sections.key_content_summary: At week 12, both groups lost significant weight, but weight loss did not differ between E-TRE+DCR and DCR. No inferential statistics were calculated for week-39 scale weights because only 13 participants per arm had measurements.

content_sections.section_title: ## Body weight and composition by DXA:
content_sections.key_content_summary: DXA weight, fat mass, and fat-free mass changes did not differ between groups at weeks 12 or 39. Mean percentage weight change at week 39 was −5.2% for E-TRE+DCR and −4.7% for DCR.
Both groups similarly reduced energy intake; week-12 energy intake and HEI did not significantly differ between groups, although HEI increased within E-TRE+DCR.
Most appetite and eating-behavior measures showed no within- or between-group differences; an isolated reduction in lunch hunger occurred in E-TRE+DCR.
The main analysis found no significant physical-activity or sedentary-time differences; a secondary pre-COVID cohort analysis identified selected within-group changes.
Adjusted resting energy expenditure did not significantly change within groups or differ between groups at week 12.
HbA1c and lipid outcomes did not differ between groups at week 12, and within-group changes were not significant.

Interprets E-TRE+DCR as acceptable but not superior to DCR for weight loss, with similar losses at weeks 12 and 39. Discusses calorie intake, meal timing, metabolic findings, COVID-related limitations, control-group eating-window reduction, and generalizability.
Directs readers to supplementary material available in the web version.
Summarizes prior evidence and highlights the study's finding that E-TRE+DCR with behavioral support produced similar clinically significant weight loss to DCR over 39 weeks.
